scenes.say: The plate arrives. Without thinking, your hands do something they've done *thousands* of times.
Fork in the left. Knife in the right. Cut, lift, *eat*.
Now picture the same moment in *Shanghai*.
A knife usually isn't part of the meal. Nobody *misses* it.
At a family meal in many *Indian* homes, the *right* hand does all the work.
And in *Bangkok*, you usually get a *spoon* and a fork. But no knife, and often no chopsticks either.
Same hunger. Same food on the plate. Completely different *tools*.
So if eating is the most *universal* thing humans do, why did we never agree on how to do it?

p.question: Why half the world doesn't use forks

scenes.say: The answer starts with a problem every cook in history has faced. And it ends somewhere you'd never expect. Inside your own *mouth*.
For most of human history, the answer was simple. Your *hands*.
Even in ancient *Rome*, a wealthy diner mostly ate with his fingers.
There were *spoons* for soup and eggs. There were forks too, but they stayed in the *kitchen*, for hauling meat out of a pot.
But hands have a limit. A roasted leg of lamb doesn't arrive in *bite-sized* pieces. Somebody has to *cut* it.
And that's where the world *splits*. Because the real question isn't what you eat with. It's where the *cutting* happens.
Let's start in *China*, where the answer was: in the *kitchen*.
Chinese cooks cut almost everything before it ever reached a *diner*.
Thin strips of meat. Diced vegetables. All of it, chopped with a single heavy *cleaver*.
Why? One popular explanation is *fuel*. Firewood was precious, and small pieces cook *fast*.
But that changes the whole meal. If the food arrives already *bite-sized*, you don't need a knife at dinner at all.
Bringing one out could seem a little *rude*, as if the cook hadn't finished the job.

p.actual: The cook already did the cutting.

scenes.say: So what do you eat with instead? Surprisingly, for a long time, the answer was a *spoon*.
Chopsticks are ancient. Archaeologists have found bone sticks in China that are *thousands* of years old, though nobody can be sure what they were used for.
And for a long time, chopsticks were the *helpers*. They fished vegetables out of soup and turned food over the fire.
The grain itself, a millet porridge, was eaten with a *spoon*.
Then, slowly, the menu changed. Wheat became more important, and with it came *noodles* and dumplings.
Try lifting a noodle with a *spoon*. Gradually, chopsticks moved to the *centre* of the meal.
From China, they travelled to *Korea*, *Japan* and *Vietnam*. And each place made them its own.
In Korea, they're often *metal*, and they still come with a *spoon*.
Legend says royalty ate with *silver* chopsticks, because silver would turn black near *poison*.
Silver really can darken when it meets certain *sulphur* compounds. But that doesn't make it a reliable poison detector.

p.actual: Silver darkens with some sulphur. It's no reliable poison detector.

scenes.say: And at the royal table, silver was also a display of *status*.
In Japan, chopsticks come with *rules*. Never stand them *upright* in a bowl of rice. That's how rice is offered to the *dead*.
And never pass food from one pair of chopsticks to *another*. At Japanese funerals, that's how family members pass the *bones* after a cremation.
So in East Asia, the cutting moved into the *kitchen*. In Europe, it stayed right there at the *table*.
European meat was often roasted in large pieces, and at a feast, the *carving* happened in front of the diners.
So diners needed a *blade*. But in the Middle Ages, your host usually didn't give you one. You brought your *own*.
Many diners carried a knife on their belt, for cutting dinner, and, if necessary, for *fighting*.
Picture it. A long table, a roast in the middle, and guests with *blades* on their belts.
Now picture *Venice*, around a thousand years ago.
Into the family of its ruler, the doge, comes a *Byzantine* noblewoman.
In Constantinople, wealthy people already ate with *forks*.
So at dinner, she has her servants cut her food into little *pieces*, and she lifts them to her mouth with a *golden* instrument with two prongs.
Decades later, a churchman named Peter *Damian* wrote about her, holding up her habits as a warning against sinful luxury. A fork. As a *warning*.

p.heard: She ate with a golden fork.
p.source: Peter Damian's letter, via the Met Museum

scenes.say: And for centuries, most of Europe kept eating with its *fingers*.
Except *Italy*. By the fourteenth century, forks were becoming common at wealthier Italian tables.
And one popular explanation will sound familiar. *Pasta*. Try eating long noodles with a knife.
By the fifteen hundreds, France's *elite* were starting to adopt the fork too. But in *England*, the idea was still strange.
Then, in *1608*, an English traveller named Thomas Coryat toured Italy, walking almost *half* of his journey.
He watched Italians eating with forks, and he helped make the habit known back *home*.
His friends gave him a nickname. *Furcifer*. Latin for fork-bearer. And also, for *rascal*.
But the fork's real breakthrough was tied to the other tool on the table. The *knife*.
Remember those pointed blades? Over time, manners changed. Pointed personal knives became less welcome at dinner, and blunt table knives became more *common*.
There's a famous story that Cardinal *Richelieu*, disgusted by a guest picking his teeth with his knife, had the tips of his own table knives ground *round*.

p.heard: A guest picks his teeth with a knife.
p.actual: Richelieu had his knives ground round.

scenes.say: And in *1669*, Louis the Fourteenth banned pointed knives in part of his kingdom.

items.name: Pointed knife
items.sub: banned in part of the kingdom

scenes.say: But a blunt knife can *cut*. It can't *spear*. Something else had to hold the food steady.
So the fork became more useful, and it changed shape. Two prongs became *three*. And by the eighteenth century, the four-pronged fork was becoming the familiar shape we recognise *today*.
And this is where the story gets *strange*.
The American anthropologist Charles Loring *Brace* spent years studying human teeth.
He noticed that most people today have an *overbite*: the top front teeth sit in front of the bottom ones.
But in old European skulls, he mostly found the teeth meeting edge to *edge*.
His explanation was this. Before knives and forks, people often *clamped* a piece of meat in their front teeth and sliced off a mouthful.
Once Europeans started cutting food into small pieces on the *plate*, the front teeth no longer had to grip. Over generations of childhoods, the bite *changed*.
Brace also pointed to evidence from Song dynasty *China*, suggesting the same change may have appeared there much earlier, among people eating pre-cut food with *chopsticks*.
But this is one researcher's explanation, not a settled *answer*. Others link it to softer food in general, going back thousands of years.

p.actual: Others point to softer food in general.

scenes.say: Still, if Brace is right, the way your ancestors cut their dinner is still written in your *face*.
And then there's the third answer, the *oldest* of all.
Eating with your hands isn't the absence of a tool. It's a tradition, with *rules*.
Across much of South Asia, the Middle East and Africa, the first rule is simple.
You eat with your *right* hand.
Often, the bread is the *cutlery*. In many Indian dining traditions, flatbread becomes a *scoop*.
In Ethiopia, the spongy bread called *injera* is the plate and the spoon at the same time.
You tear, you fold, you *lift*.
There's even a gesture for *love*. In Ethiopia, it's called *gursha*.
You take a mouthful, and you feed it to someone else, with your own *hand*. A guest, an elder, a newly married partner.
And here's a twist. *Thailand* used to eat with hands too.
Then, during the eighteen hundreds, Siam's royal court and elites began adopting Western *spoons* and *forks*.
Then the habit spread. Today, the spoon goes in your *right* hand, and the fork pushes food onto it.
That's why there's no knife, and usually no *chopsticks*.

p.actual: Just a spoon and a fork.

scenes.say: So where does that leave the stories you've probably *heard*?
Here is the story you heard. *Confucius* banned knives from the dinner table, because knives meant violence.
What's true? There is a famous Chinese saying: a gentleman keeps away from the *kitchen*.
What's wrong? It comes from *Mencius*, not Confucius.
And in context, he's talking about a king who couldn't bear to see an *ox* led to its death. It's about *compassion*, not table manners.
Here's another. *Catherine* de' Medici brought the fork from Italy to France. It's a lovely story.
Historians aren't *convinced*. The evidence is thin.

p.heard: She brought the fork to France.

scenes.say: And the biggest one of all. That forks are simply the *civilised* way to eat. Europe spent *six centuries* thinking the opposite.
And every tradition in this story comes with manners just as strict as any dinner party in *Paris*.
None of these tools is *better*. Each one is a smart answer to a different *problem*.
So let's go back to that *plate*.
The round tip on your knife? Centuries of changing table manners, and maybe one fussy *cardinal*.
The four prongs on your fork? The seventeen *hundreds*.
And the cutting you're about to do, right there at the table? That's Europe's *answer*, from a time when diners brought their own blades.
In Shanghai, the cutting happened hours ago, in a *kitchen*.
In Addis Ababa, the *bread* is doing the work.
And in *Bangkok*, the spoon and fork began at a royal court in the eighteen hundreds.
Same problem. How do you get food from the plate to your mouth? Three brilliant *answers*.
And one of them may even be shaping your *teeth*.

And if you're wondering why a *Korean* meal so often comes glowing red with chili, while a *Japanese* meal usually doesn't, that's a story about a plant that crossed the world. And it starts in the *Americas*.

p.title: A plant that crossed the world
